title: Rehearsing new arrangements and memorising them
summary: Process of learning new numbers by sections and memorising, with Armstrong's memory.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Were your arrangements easy to play?

Well, you'd get used to them, yeah. You'd get used to them, sure. We'd take, when we came off the road from the least one night, as we'd go on the road saying, Joe Green would build a tune for us for two months. The Easton tune, the Western tune, and the Southern tune, and all that sort of stuff. When we'd come back, we'd buy new arrangements, different tunes. Now, we'd take a number. The reeds would get into this side of the hall, or wherever we were rehearsing. The brass gets over, the trombones get over there, the trumpet's over here, and the rhythm section stays with the piano. And we'd just run over to get the notes together. Then when we got it, in about a half an hour, we'd say, all right, you fellas ready, you're here. But then we'd go up, we'd play it for the sound, to see what's happening. We'd play the tune that's written. Then the ideas start coming, and the pops would say, well, the second chorus, Nick, you'd take the first 16 balls, or the middle of the chorus, or whatever it is. And I'd check it off. And then when the trombone, Hickey, take that, and Charlie Holmes, you'd take this, and Red Allen, you'd take this, and pops would take the rest. And then, we'd run over it like that. Then when we'd get it down, two or three times, we'd put that number aside, we'd take the album. We'd just rehearse two numbers. And at night, when we'd playin' on the job, in the first set, we'd put one of those numbers in the set, in the middle part some way. And before we'd close, we'd play it again. And after we didn't eat the music, we'd memorize, we'd show up on memorizing. That's the main thing. Louie is the greatest musician I know for memorizing. He was fantastic. This man would take a tune he'd never seen before. He'd stick his handkerchief in his trumpet, and he's concentrating on the notes. And when he'd say, all right, pops, we're ready, you're it. He'd go up there, and he might put the part up at rehearsal. At night, memorizing, you know, just that quick.
